subject: lavaan and PROCESS inconsistencies in the 95% CI

messages.author: b66e6bf52a2ceb6c
messages.subject: lavaan and PROCESS inconsistencies in the 95% CI
parts:
Hi there,
I ran an analysis using model 80 from Process, and created the same model in Lavaan. All of my coefficients are the same, and the standard errors are the same. I run into trouble when I try to get the bootstrapped 95% CI. I used the same number of bootstrapped samples, and have run it a couple of times, but still find inconsistencies. Has anyone had this issue?

messages.author: 189d19347ab44a74
messages.subject: Re: lavaan and PROCESS inconsistencies in the 95% CI
parts:
I am not familiar with Process model 80, but there are several issues here.

  1. It could be that the bootstrapping technique or the correction are not identical.
  2. Even if they are identical, without setting a seed you shouldn’t expect them to be identical. A seed allows you to set the random number generator. A bootstrapped sample is a done by taking a random sample with replacement from your data of size N (where N is the number of observations in your original data set). So, it’s stochastic and should vary.

How different are your results? Are your estimates the same just the CIs differ? Can you provide more info about Process model 80 as well as the R code your running and maybe a reproducible amount of data/code?

Chris

messages.subject: Re: lavaan and PROCESS inconsistencies in the 95% CI
parts:
Thanks for getting back to me!
1. I think they should both be bias-corrected (and that's it). PROCESS does that be default, and I selected the "bca.simple" option for bootstrapping in parameterEstimates. I guess it is possible that there are differences beyond that, but I'm not sure how to figure that out.

2. I think this may be the explanation...the estimates are entirely the same, the CIs are just very slightly different (never by more than 1/1000). I'm attaching the visual depiction of model 80, as well as my code (note that in my code, I have five intermediary mediators, not just two). X=combinedses, Y=externt, my Mk=all, covariates are race and sex, and the other variables are all Ms that come before Mk. Sorry that's a convoluted way to describe it! I can't really attach reproducible code with the data since it's proprietary and I have it through a datasharing agreement, but hopefully this is clear enough. 



multipleMediation2 <- '
    externt ~  d*combinedses + c*all+e1*parentatt + e2*goodneighborhood + e3*famdynz + e4*goodmonitoring+ e5*school+sex +race
    all ~ b1 * parentatt + b2*goodneighborhood  +b3*famdynz+b4*goodmonitoring+b5*school+b6*combinedses + sex  + race

    parentatt~a1*combinedses + sex +race
    goodneighborhood~a2*combinedses + sex +race 
    famdynz~a3*combinedses + sex +race 
    goodmonitoring~a4*combinedses + sex + race
   school~a5*combinedses + sex + race 

    indirect1 :=  a1*e1
    indirect2 := a2*e2
    indirect3 :=a3*e3
    indirect4 :=a4*e4
    indirect5 :=a5*e5
    indirect6 :=b6*c
    indirect7 := a1*b1*c
    indirect8 := a2*b2*c
    indirect9 := a3*b3*c
    indirect10 := a4*b4*c
    indirect11 := a5*b5*c
    totalindirect :=(a1 *e1) + (a2 *e2)+ (a3*e3)+(a4*e4)+(a5*e5)+(b6*c)+(a1*b1*c)+
(a2*b2*c)+(a3*b3*c)+(a4*b4*c)+(a5*b5*c)
    total    := d+ (a1 *e1) + (a2 *e2)+ (a3*e3)+(a4*e4)+(a5*e5)+(b6*c)+(a1*b1*c)+
(a2*b2*c)+(a3*b3*c)+(a4*b4*c)+(a5*b5*c)
'

fit2 <- sem(multipleMediation2, data=z, se="bootstrap",
            bootstrap=10000)
summary(fit2, standardized=TRUE, fit.measures=TRUE)
parameterEstimates(fit2, zstat=TRUE, boot.ci.type = "bca.simple", rsquare=TRUE)
----------------------
